# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

## A bookend

Title: `refactor: extract config loader opening`

```
Opens the cycle "refactor: extract config loader". Its record is the
In Progress block in TODO.md.
```

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the
cycle by its title and pointing at its record. The closing's body is the same shape with "Closes".

136:### Commit-body form
137-
138-The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
139-shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
140-problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
141-bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
142-statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
143-
144-- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
145-  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
146-  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
147-  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
148-  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
149-- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
150-  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
151-  to be more than one commit.
152-- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
153-  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
154-  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
155-- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
156-  form, the general form at its smallest.
157-- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
158-  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
159-  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.
160-
161-**The markers are typed on purpose**: `*` always means problem, `-` always means solution, and the
162-pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The
163-typing also keeps history greppable (`^\* ` finds every facet, `^ - ` every solution). Bodies are
164-read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
165-flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
166-a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.
167-
168-Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
169-[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit).
170-
171-### Semicolons
172-
173-Prose carries no semicolons. A semicolon appears only in code (code spans, fenced code, source

138-The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
139-shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
140-problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
141-bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
142-statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.
143-
144-- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
145-  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
146-  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
147-  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
148-  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
149-- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
150-  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
151-  to be more than one commit.
152-- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
153-  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
154-  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.

156-  form, the general form at its smallest.

158-  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,

# Doing: the cycle record

What is being done: the running cycle's planning and its work's documentation. The last
finished cycle's is in [zCLOSED.md](zCLOSED.md), and what we might do is in [TODO.md](TODO.md). The
block's shape is on trial: it opens with the Todo as it was picked from `TODO.md`, then the
Deliberation, the plan, Solution and Acceptance check, and the Ladder with its details.

This file is a trial (2026-10-09). The agent-files still name `TODO.md > ## In Progress` as the
record's home, and the cycle that makes this file the rule is [The cycle-record moves out of
TODO.md into zDOING.md](TODO.md#the-cycle-record-moves-out-of-todomd-into-zdoingmd).

## Continuation notes

Where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a record: read first, acted
on, and reset to `_None._` by the reader. Kept here by the trial and no longer in `TODO.md`,
where [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint) still says to look.

(agent, 2026-10-13) The cycle below is one rung short of closed.

- The cycle `docs: the session lock` is in flight on the bookmark `docs-the-session-lock`, its
  fourth rung pushed. The next step is the closing rung, at version 0.84.27.
  - The closing replaces the record in `zCLOSED.md` with the block below.
  - Its Land is a trapezoid, wink's call, on a go of its own: the closing gets two parents,
    `docs: update single-step cycle add zCLOSED.md` first and the fourth rung second, and `main`
    moves forward onto it.

## In Progress

### docs: the session lock

(wink + agent, 2026-10-12) No Todo entry was picked for managing a session lock. The first entry
held two plans, the lock `vc-x1` takes for a run and what the session lock, `.agent-running`,
left undone, and the cycle began as a rewrite of the second. The rewrite asked for a hook that
takes the lock in the agent's place, and a day of looking into that ended in a decision not to
build one.

The session lock was added as two single-step cycles, each landing on `main`. This cycle gathers
those two with what was found today into one ladder and closes it as a trapezoid.

#### Deliberation

- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`, wink's call.
  - Two sessions were tested with no lock, wink's thought, to see what the lock is worth:
    pushes minutes apart, pushes in the same second, and one session resumed in two terminals.
  - Nothing either session wrote was lost, and every transcript line parses, but the commit
    title and bodies might be missing if they happened at the same time with the first one
    committing all the work that both did.
  - One line of instruction prevents that. What was found is in
    [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md), not here.
- The agent keeps taking the lock itself. Two other takers were considered, a Claude Code hook
  and `vc-x1`, and neither is built, wink's call.
  - A hook is a command Claude Code runs on its own when a session starts, so the lock would
    not depend on an agent reading the instruction and following it. A trial showed a hook can
    take the lock and hold it for as long as the session runs.
  - The hook is not built because it needs `CLAUDE_PID`, the id of the Claude Code process, to
    know when the session has ended. Claude Code's documents do not name that variable, so any
    release could drop it.
  - `vc-x1` taking the lock was thought to close a gap between the agent's probe and its hold.
    It closes none, wink's point: one asker wins a `flock`, whichever program asks.
- The current top two commits on main are being converted from being single-step
  cycles into a multi-step trapezoid, because in retrospect it should have been multi-step
  from the start, wink's call 2026-10-12.
  - Nothing published is rewritten. The two keep their ids, titles, and trailers, and the
    closing descends from both, so `main` moves forward onto it.
  - It is an exception to [Cycle shape](AGENTS.md#cycle-shape), where a single-step cycle
    lands as it is. It covers these two commits and the versions below, and Land takes its
    own go.
- Every rung has a bare version, 0.84.25 and 0.84.26 for the two rungs made in the cycle and
  0.84.27 for the closing.
  - The first two landed bare, 0.84.23 and 0.84.24, and are published.
  - A suffixed version wants the `-dev` name beside it, and the cycle is documents alone.
- A fourth rung is inserted ahead of the closing, wink's call, 2026-10-13
  ([Unplanned work](AGENTS.md#unplanned-work)).
  - The closing's review grew Todo planning that is no bookkeeping: `TODO.md` lost the headings
    the record left behind, and two entries were reworked.
  - The closing's own edits were set aside while the rung was made, so each commit has its own
    change alone.
  - It is outside the cycle's subject and is a rung all the same, the edits being made and
    reviewed, and a cycle of its own costing an opening, a closing, and a Land.

The session lock stays as it is. What a hook could do and what two sessions do without a lock are
written down in a notes file, three Todo entries carry what is left, and a closing merge draws
the trapezoid around the lock's commits.

225:### The per-rung flow
226-
227-Every commit (opening, each rung between, closing) goes through these steps, read from here
228-immediately before acting ([why](agent-data/rationale.md#the-per-rung-flow)):
229-
230-1. Mark current: mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
231-2. Bump: bump the version-of-record to this commit's version ([Suffix
232-   scheme](agent-data/versioning.md#suffix-scheme)), the agent-files version beside it in an
233-   `agent-files` proposal cycle.
234-3. Work: do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop ([Stop and
235-   ask](#stop-and-ask)).
236-4. Rung subsection: write what this rung changed, conceptually, into its subsection under the
237-   ladder. The rung stays `(current)` until step 7.
238-5. Validate: `vc-x1 validate` before every review, doc-only commits included. The full run rewrites
239-   files (`cargo fmt`), so use `--fast` while a review iterates.
240-6. Work review: stop before writing any description and say "please review", as its own message with
241-   no title or body. Iterate until the user says "continue" / "go". The review is of the
242-   working-copy diff ([jj basics](agent-data/jj.md#jj-basics)).
243-7. Flip and describe: flip `(current)` to `(done)` the moment "done" is true, then write the
244-   description in [Commit-body form](agent-data/prose.md#commit-body-form), read from the file first
245-   with its specimen, [commit-model.md](agent-data/commit-model.md) ([Commit
246-   description](#commit-description)).
247-8. Description review: show the title + body and stop. Ask permission to commit and push without
248-   spelling out the invocation. The go covers the push only when it says so.
249-9. Commit + push: on the go, `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."` ([Committing vs
250-   pushing](#committing-vs-pushing)), then [At rest](#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push).

### The session lock is proposed to the set, and its instruction has two faults

(wink + agent, 2026-10-12) The session lock, `.agent-running`, is an instruction in this project's
`custom.md` and nowhere else. What it is, and what two sessions do without it, is in
[session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md).

- Propose the lock to the set, convention work and so a cycle of its own. `flock` is a Linux
  tool and the instruction is this project's, and both want an answer first.
  - macOS has the `flock` call and does not ship the tool, and Windows has neither.
  - We think the answer is a small `vc-x1` command that takes the lock and holds it, through
    Rust's `File::try_lock`: `flock` on Linux and macOS, `LockFileEx` on Windows, and each
    system drops the lock when the holder dies.
  - That is code in `vc-x1` for the session lock, which the cycle that tested two sessions
    decided against. It weighed races and not other systems.
- The instruction has two faults, and neither has a fix planned:
  - A session that has forgotten it holds the lock probes again at a reacquaint, fails against
    its own holder, and stops as if another session held it.
  - An edit to the instruction reaches only the sessions started after it.
- A hook that takes the lock in the agent's place was designed and not built, wink's call, the
  same file saying why.

### vc-x1 takes a lock of its own for every run

# Closed: the last cycle's record

The last finished cycle's record, whole. A cycle's closing replaces this file's `## Closed` with
its own block from [zDOING.md](zDOING.md) and this file's references with that block's, so the
last record stays here until the next one is finished. Earlier cycles are in each landmark
commit's copy of the record.

## Closed

### docs: the session lock

(wink + agent, 2026-10-12) No Todo entry was picked for managing a session lock. The first entry
held two plans, the lock `vc-x1` takes for a run and what the session lock, `.agent-running`,
left undone, and the cycle began as a rewrite of the second. The rewrite asked for a hook that
takes the lock in the agent's place, and a day of looking into that ended in a decision not to
build one.

The session lock was added as two single-step cycles, each landing on `main`. This cycle gathers
those two with what was found today into one ladder and closes it as a trapezoid.

#### Deliberation

- The lock stays as the instruction in `custom.md`, wink's call.
  - Two sessions were tested with no lock, wink's thought, to see what the lock is worth:
    pushes minutes apart, pushes in the same second, and one session resumed in two terminals.
  - Nothing either session wrote was lost, and every transcript line parses, but the commit
    title and bodies might be missing if they happened at the same time with the first one
    committing all the work that both did.
  - One line of instruction prevents that. What was found is in
    [session-lock.md](notes/session-lock.md), not here.
- The agent keeps taking the lock itself. Two other takers were considered, a Claude Code hook
  and `vc-x1`, and neither is built, wink's call.
  - A hook is a command Claude Code runs on its own when a session starts, so the lock would
    not depend on an agent reading the instruction and following it. A trial showed a hook can
    take the lock and hold it for as long as the session runs.
  - The hook is not built because it needs `CLAUDE_PID`, the id of the Claude Code process, to
    know when the session has ended. Claude Code's documents do not name that variable, so any
    release could drop it.
  - `vc-x1` taking the lock was thought to close a gap between the agent's probe and its hold.
    It closes none, wink's point: one asker wins a `flock`, whichever program asks.
- The current top two commits on main are being converted from being single-step
  cycles into a multi-step trapezoid, because in retrospect it should have been multi-step
  from the start, wink's call 2026-10-12.
  - Nothing published is rewritten. The two keep their ids, titles, and trailers, and the
    closing descends from both, so `main` moves forward onto it.
  - It is an exception to [Cycle shape](AGENTS.md#cycle-shape), where a single-step cycle
    lands as it is. It covers these two commits and the versions below, and Land takes its
    own go.

## Cycle bookmarks: create and land

The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).

**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
and the bookmark derive from one bare title):

- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
  ready to be seen.

**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Every
`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):

1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
   (`@` sits directly above it).
2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
   as it is.
3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
   cycle anymore.
5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
   disposal once fully merged.

- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.

**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so [No re-describe without
  coordinating](#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer) stays intact.
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions**, named and moved past: the bookmark has already landed, another branch is stacked
  on it, or the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.

## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged

A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark: it
carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its only
holder.

- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference
- coordinated rebases stay available (the bar is on unilateral rewrites, not rewrites), at the known
  cost of staling the git-SHA citations in the records. Chids and ochid trailers survive a rebase
- once the bookmark's history is fully merged into `main` the bookmark is redundant and is deleted,
  locally and remotely

The contrast with a cycle bookmark is the whole point: that one is a draft and may be rewritten
freely until it lands (see [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)), this
one is published and may not. Refined 2026-08-03 from the earlier "treated as permanent, never
rebased" wording, after a fully merged long-lived bookmark was deleted without loss.

## Close-out shapes

The two shapes a ladder can land in, chosen by the user and recorded at close-out, executed at
[Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) ([Close-out](../AGENTS.md#close-out)). A single-step cycle
is one commit and lands as it is:

- **trapezoid**, the current default: a merge commit whose first parent is the trunk and whose
  second is the ladder, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while every rung
  stays reachable. Reshaped at Land by the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe) and published
  by the landing fast-forward itself.
- **keep separate**, one commit per rung on `main`, when the decomposition itself is informative.

Squash is not a shape: each rung's `ochid:` trailer is a change id, a squash keeps one and drops the
rest, and every agent-repo commit that pointed at a dropped rung is left dangling ([Cycle
shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)).

**Preview before choosing.** The cycle's net change is the tree diff from `<base>` to the tip,
whatever shape the commits between are in: `jj diff --from <base> --to <tip>`, or the gitk range
described in [Read a change in gitk at full context](#read-a-change-in-gitk-at-full-context). The
trapezoid keeps each rung reachable while `git log --first-parent` shows this net diff once landed,
and keep separate shows the rungs themselves. The choice is made on what `main` will carry.

## Read a change in gitk at full context

gitk renders a change three ways, and at full context each answers a different question. Raise
"Lines of context" to the longest file's length, or to a large number such as 1000 (`--context 1000`
is the CLI equivalent), to see the entire file, then select:

- **New version**: the file as it now is, with the added lines lit. This is what the permanent
  branch will carry, so it is the view for judging whether a change reads as one thing.
- **Old version**: the file as it was, with the removed lines lit. It answers what the change costs,
  which a diff states only as minus lines out of context.
- **Diff**: the two interleaved. At full context it is the whole file with the edit marked in place,
  which is the reading a reviewer wants when the edit is small and the file is not.

The above reads one commit at a time and is useful. Another mode is to see how several commits
together changed the tree since a given `<base>` commit. To do that:

- Hover over the commit you want as the `<base>`, right click and select "Mark this commit".
- Hover over any commit above the `<base>`, right click and select "Diff marked commit -> this".

Now New version, Old version and Diff show the net change of everything between `<base>` and `this`.
If `<base>` is the parent of the `opening` commit and `this` is the `closing`, that is the cycle's
net change, and it can help you decide what shape to choose ([Close-out shapes](#close-out-shapes)).

## Trapezoid close-out recipe

The reshape behind the trapezoid shape, run at [Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) step 2: the
close-out commit, pushed linearly by the closing rung, becomes a merge whose first parent is the
trunk line and whose second parent is the cycle's ladder. Nothing here publishes, the merge goes out
with Land's fast-forward.

```
  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
                      \                    /
  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
```

- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle opened. It
  becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a cycle landed linearly since
  (keep-separate shape, or a single-step cycle) sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, reshaped here.

1. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent
   order is the argument order.
2. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its own.
   What step 1 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants onto the
   rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` lands beside the merge on `<tip>` and the tree
   reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
3. Verify two parents: `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
   both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>` is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at
   three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from a correct one in
   `jj log --no-graph`.

Details:

- **Trailers survive.** The restore's squash and the reshape change `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its
  change id, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped at the closing push stay valid in both directions.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed: a topic bookmark's commits are not on `trunk()` until Land's
  fast-forward.

Recovery:

- **Nothing is published until Land's fast-forward**, so the whole reshape is undoable with
  `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge**: undo and redo step 1 with the corrected revisions. Do not
  land a shape you did not intend. After the fast-forward the remote boundary is crossed and
  recovery is forward-only.
- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 2 skipped): `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Any
  commit made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a rebase onto the merge.

file.content:
## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If Rust,
  `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and leaves plain
  `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
  install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit flow's
  install.

**Single-name variant**: a repo striving to release makes the package name the binary's name, plain
`<name>` on `main` only:

- **The opening renames**: its bump sets `<name>-dev` beside the suffixed version, and every rung
  and the closing build under the dev name, the closing over the bare version.
- **Land restores**: the rename back to `<name>` is Land's act, so the stable name is only ever
  installed from what `main` will carry.
- **A build script guards the pairing** on every cargo verb: a suffixed version under the stable
  name fails the build, so no mid-cycle install can clobber the consumers' binary.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

It means making the `vc-x1` binary on your `PATH` the one built from what `main` now carries. For a Rust project that is `cargo install --path . --locked`, run with the work-repo at `main`.

Why it is a Land step at all: in a normal cycle the opening renames the package to `vc-x1-dev`, so every mid-cycle `vc-x1 validate` installs `vc-x1-dev` and leaves your working `vc-x1` alone. Land renames it back, and only then is the plain `vc-x1` installed, from the landed code. "The artifact" is the agent-files' word for the built product, here that binary.

For this cycle it is already done. The cycle is documents only and ran under bare versions with no `-dev` rename, so each `vc-x1 validate` installed plain `vc-x1` as its fourth command. The last one ran at the closing, and the installed binary reports `vc-x1 0.84.27`, the version `main` now has. The reshape into a merge changed no file, so the installed build matches `main`'s tree.

So there is nothing to run for that step. What is left of Land:

- delete the bookmark `docs-the-session-lock`, locally and on origin, which is a push and needs your go
- check acceptance line 4, `jj log -r 'main@origin..main'` printing nothing
